paragraphs: An autoencoder can do more than reconstruct an input once: repeatedly feeding its output back into itself can create a memory-retrieval process. The relevant behavior is attraction, where repeated applications move inputs toward a stored example. This paper analyzes when overparameterized networks with sigmoid activations can exhibit that behavior.

The analysis uses the connection between infinitely wide neural networks and kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel. This gives the authors a theoretical way to study the trained network’s input-output Jacobian, which describes how small input changes affect its output. Earlier work identified eigenvalue magnitudes strictly below one as a condition supporting associative memory through iteration.

The authors show that attractors can exist in this infinite-width setting for both single-example and multiple-example training, under specified conditions. With multiple examples, they find that increasing input norm can push the largest Jacobian eigenvalue magnitude below one. The result connects input scale and local stability to memory behavior; it does not claim that every trained sigmoid autoencoder automatically becomes an associative memory.
icml-2020-associative-memory-in-iterated.tldr: The paper identifies conditions under which infinitely wide sigmoid autoencoders can retrieve memories through repeated application.

paragraphs: Understanding how neural networks handle incorrect labels requires experiments in which the amount of label noise can be controlled. The paper argues that earlier controlled studies relied on artificially corrupted labels because suitable real-world datasets were unavailable. This left a gap between studying synthetic errors and studying the label errors encountered in web data.

Its first contribution is a benchmark that makes real-world web label noise controllable for experimental study. The authors also introduce a simple method intended to handle both synthetic and real label noise. They report the best results among the evaluated approaches on their dataset and on the CIFAR and WebVision benchmarks.

The third contribution is a broad investigation spanning different noise levels, types of noise, network architectures, and training settings. Together, these contributions make the paper both a method proposal and a resource for examining noisy-label learning. Its significance is the ability to compare behavior across controlled conditions while including noise originating from real web data, rather than drawing conclusions solely from synthetic corruption.
icml-2020-beyond-synthetic-noise-deep-le.tldr: The paper introduces controlled real-world label-noise experiments, a robust training method, and a broad study of learning with incorrect labels.

paragraphs: Sequential experimental design asks which experiment to perform next when only a limited sequence of experiments is available. An ideal decision would account for how today’s observation changes later choices. Computing that policy generally requires intractable Bellman equations, so common approximations consider only the next step and can give exploration too little weight.

BINOCULARS approximates longer-horizon reasoning through a batch calculation. It first computes a batch of experiments that is optimal for a one-step batch objective, then chooses a single member of that batch to evaluate. This lets information about a collection of experiments influence the next sequential choice without directly solving the full optimal-policy problem.

The authors apply the framework to Bayesian optimization and Bayesian quadrature, which have substantially different objectives. They report significant improvements over myopic alternatives in real-world scenarios. The contribution is therefore a general recipe for making sequential choices less shortsighted, with demonstrated applications to both problems, while retaining an approximation rather than claiming to compute the exact optimal experimental policy.
icml-2020-binoculars-for-efficient-nonmy.tldr: BINOCULARS uses an optimized batch of experiments to choose one next experiment with a broader planning perspective.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering turns pairwise judgments into groups. A classifier labels graph edges as similar or dissimilar, and a clustering pays for disagreements: similar pairs separated into different groups and dissimilar pairs placed together. Edge weights determine how costly each disagreement is, so the objective accounts for unequal consequences of different classification errors.

The paper studies a particular asymmetry in those weights. Similar edges must have weights between alpha times a positive scale w and w, while dissimilar edges must have weights at least alpha times w. Under this assumption, the authors give an algorithm whose disagreement cost is within a factor of 3 + 2 ln(1/alpha) of the optimum.

The guarantee becomes weaker as alpha decreases and the permitted weight imbalance grows. The authors also establish a linear-programming integrality gap growing as ln(1/alpha), asymptotically matching the approximation’s dependence on that parameter. This identifies a corresponding limitation of the relaxation, rather than proving that every possible clustering algorithm must incur the same approximation factor.
icml-2020-correlation-clustering-with-as.tldr: The paper gives a clustering approximation guarantee under asymmetric edge-weight assumptions and a matching-order linear-programming integrality gap.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides a geometrically meaningful way to compare distributions and form their barycenters, or distributional averages. Entropy regularization makes these computations much cheaper through Sinkhorn’s algorithm, but it also introduces smoothing. For barycenters, that computational convenience can appear as unwanted blur in the resulting average.

The paper connects this smoothing bias closely to the reference measure used to define the entropy regularizer. Using that connection, the authors propose debiased Sinkhorn barycenters that retain fast Sinkhorn-like iterations while removing entropy smoothing. The aim is to preserve the computational benefits that made regularized optimal transport attractive in the first place.

The theoretical result establishes perfect debiasing for Gaussian distributions with equal variance. That condition matters: the abstract does not extend the exact guarantee to every family of distributions. Experiments illustrate reduced blurring together with a computational advantage. The work thus supplies both a precise special-case guarantee and empirical support for computing sharper barycenters without abandoning the efficient iterative approach.
icml-2020-debiased-sinkhorn-barycenters-.tldr: Debiased Sinkhorn barycenters reduce entropy-induced blur while retaining fast iterations, with exact debiasing proved for equal-variance Gaussians.

paragraphs: Correctly classifying every training example does not mean the training loss has reached zero. A network can keep lowering its loss by becoming more confident in predictions it already gets right. The paper addresses the resulting overconfidence and degraded test performance by directly controlling how low the training loss is allowed to go.

The proposed method, flooding, sets a small positive target called the flood level. Training follows ordinary mini-batch gradient descent when the loss is above that level and switches to gradient ascent when it falls below. This makes the loss fluctuate around the target. The change requires one line of code and can be combined with stochastic optimizers and other regularizers.

The authors expect this continued movement at nonzero loss to carry the network toward flatter parts of the loss landscape that generalize better. That explanation is presented as an expectation, while performance improvements are demonstrated experimentally. The experiments also show a double-descent pattern in test loss as a byproduct of flooding.
icml-2020-do-we-need-zero-training-loss-.tldr: Flooding improves generalization experimentally by keeping training loss near a small positive level instead of continually driving it toward zero.

paragraphs: Finding a Nash equilibrium is an optimization problem involving several interacting players, including the competing models used in GAN training. Extra-gradient methods use gradient extrapolations before making updates. This paper asks whether those operations need to involve every player at every iteration, particularly when the number of players is large.

The proposed method performs extrapolations and updates on a randomly chosen subset of players. For nonsmooth convex games with noisy gradient information, the authors prove a better convergence rate than full extra-gradient. They also introduce a variance-reduction mechanism to obtain speedups in smooth convex games, treating that setting separately from the nonsmooth result.

Sampling makes extrapolation more manageable in games with many participants. Experiments show speedups, especially with a heuristic that samples players cyclically, and the authors report faster and better training of GANs and mixtures of GANs. These empirical findings broaden the practical motivation, while the stated convergence improvement remains tied to the convex-game and gradient-noise conditions used in the analysis.
icml-2020-extra-gradient-with-player-sam.tldr: Updating sampled players in extra-gradient methods improves convergence under stated game assumptions and speeds up GAN training empirically.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent usually learns with a fixed menu of actions. When that menu changes, the agent may need expensive retraining even if its broader goal remains similar. This paper introduces zero-shot generalization to new actions as a problem in its own right: choosing effectively when previously unseen action options become available.

The proposed framework has two stages. First, the agent infers representations of actions from information acquired separately from the task. It then learns a policy that can accommodate varying action sets, using objectives intended to encourage generalization. The separation lets action information inform decision-making without requiring every action to have appeared during task training.

The authors benchmark this capability on sequential tasks that include solving physical reasoning puzzles with an unseen set of tools and stacking towers using novel three-dimensional shapes. These tasks make the changing action set central to the challenge. The paper’s stated contribution is the problem formulation, framework, and benchmark evaluation; the abstract does not assert a universal ability to handle arbitrary new actions.
icml-2020-generalization-to-new-actions-.tldr: The paper trains policies to handle new action choices by combining separately learned action representations with objectives for generalization.

paragraphs: Generating molecular graphs from individual atoms or small cycles can become less effective as molecules grow larger. The authors demonstrate substantial performance degradation for earlier approaches in that setting. Their response is to use larger, more flexible structural motifs as building blocks, making molecular generation operate at several levels of detail.

The encoder builds a fine-to-coarse representation, starting with atoms and progressing to connected motifs. At each level, it combines information from the smaller constituents with the graph structure at that level. The decoder reverses this direction: it constructs a molecule one motif at a time, alternating between choosing a motif and deciding how to attach it.

This hierarchy connects detailed molecular information with decisions about larger pieces of structure. The authors evaluate the model on several molecule-generation tasks, including polymers, and report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support using richer building blocks for the evaluated generation problems, particularly in the context of the difficulties they identify with larger molecules.
icml-2020-hierarchical-generation-of-mol.tldr: A hierarchical molecular generator builds graphs from larger structural motifs and significantly improves results on evaluated tasks, including polymers.

paragraphs: Variance-reduced optimization methods can have strong theoretical guarantees yet remain slow because they periodically estimate gradients using large batches. Adjusting batch size offers a way to reduce that expense. Existing approaches either follow a predetermined schedule or inspect the optimization path through extra backtracking and condition-checking steps.

This paper proposes choosing batch sizes using stochastic gradients already collected during optimization. The method therefore responds to the observed optimization history without requiring a backtracking line search. Its central idea is to use past gradient information to guide how much data should be used for subsequent gradient estimation.

The authors develop a convergence-analysis framework that handles the dependence between batch size and earlier stochastic gradients. They show substantial reductions in overall complexity for SVRG and SARAH/SPIDER in both conventional nonconvex optimization and reinforcement-learning problems. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of the adaptation scheme. The contribution combines a practical way to avoid extra search steps with theoretical treatment of the history dependence that the adaptive rule introduces.
icml-2020-history-gradient-aided-batch-s.tldr: Using past stochastic gradients to adapt batch sizes reduces the complexity of variance-reduced optimization without backtracking line searches.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation must transfer a model to a target domain without target labels. Class-conditioned alignment tries to match corresponding classes across domains, often using estimated target labels called pseudo-labels. The paper focuses on practical difficulties when classes are imbalanced within a domain or their relative frequencies differ between domains.

Directly optimizing a loss built from pseudo-labels can accumulate errors when those labels are wrong. The authors instead use pseudo-labels to guide which samples are selected, producing alignment implicitly through sampling. Pseudo-labels still influence training, but the method removes the need to optimize model parameters explicitly against them as target labels.

The theoretical analysis identifies a shortcut available to a domain discriminator when classes are misaligned, and the proposed approach addresses that shortcut to support adversarial domain learning. Experiments and ablations confirm effectiveness, particularly under class imbalance and shifts in class distributions. The result highlights sample selection as an alternative way to use uncertain class information when aligning domains.
icml-2020-implicit-class-conditioned-dom.tldr: The method uses pseudo-label-guided sampling for implicit class alignment, improving domain adaptation especially under class imbalance and distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Random-feature models approximate kernel methods using a finite collection of features. This paper examines how that approximation changes the predictor, beyond simply making computation more manageable. Using random matrix theory, the authors relate Gaussian random-feature regression to kernel ridge regression, which explicitly regularizes the fitted model through a ridge parameter.

For a model with P features, N observations, and ridge parameter lambda, the expected random-feature predictor is close to a kernel predictor with an effective ridge larger than lambda. As the number of features increases, that effective ridge decreases monotonically toward lambda. Finite feature sampling therefore introduces additional regularization even when the explicit ridge setting stays fixed.

The authors also derive an explicit bound comparing the effective-ridge kernel predictor’s test error with the average risk of the random-feature predictor. Empirically, they find very close agreement between the test errors of the averaged random-feature predictor and the corresponding kernel predictor. The distinction between an expected predictor and an individual random realization matters to interpreting these results.
icml-2020-implicit-regularization-of-ran.tldr: Finite Gaussian random-feature sampling acts like additional ridge regularization, with its strength decreasing as more features are used.

paragraphs: Different local minima of a neural network’s training objective can differ in how well they generalize. The paper brings together two questions that are often treated separately: how to recognize solutions that generalize well, and how to steer training toward such solutions. It proposes a single information-theoretic quantity for both purposes.

That quantity is based on observed Fisher information. The authors present it as a metric strongly indicative of a local minimum’s generalization behavior and also turn it into a practical regularizer. This links assessment and intervention: the same underlying measure helps characterize a trained solution and influences the process used to obtain one.

The theoretical analysis includes a generalization bound, while experiments evaluate both the metric’s descriptive role and its use in improving generalization. The evaluations cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with multiple network architectures. The reported findings support this unified approach across those experiments, without making the metric an infallible predictor of generalization for every network or minimum.
icml-2020-information-theoretic-local-mi.tldr: An observed-Fisher-information metric both characterizes generalization at local minima and serves as a regularizer that improves it empirically.

paragraphs: Making an informed decision involves choosing what evidence to collect, how much to spend collecting it, and when to stop. Active sensing studies those choices in pursuit of a goal. Inverse active sensing starts with observed behavior and asks what preferences and strategy could explain an agent’s sequence of information gathering and commitment.

The paper develops a unified framework for these problems when time pressure arises within the decision setting and depends on context. It represents subjective tradeoffs among accuracy, speed, and information cost. This makes the timing of a decision part of the strategy being modeled, alongside which observations to acquire and which final decision to make.

For the forward problem, the framework expresses intuitive concepts such as surprise, suspense, and optimality in decision strategies. For the inverse problem, the authors illustrate how it can quantify preferences implicit in observed strategies. The contribution is a shared mathematical language for constructing decision models and interpreting behavior through the tradeoffs those models represent.
icml-2020-inverse-active-sensing-modelin.tldr: The paper models evidence gathering under time pressure and uses observed decisions to infer preferences about accuracy, speed, and information cost.

paragraphs: The paper studies episodic decision-making with three difficulties at once: unknown state transitions, losses chosen adversarially, and bandit feedback that provides only limited information about losses. Each episode has a finite horizon. The learner must improve its decisions while learning the environment’s dynamics and working with incomplete feedback.

The algorithm combines a tighter confidence set for the transition function with an optimistic loss estimator. That estimator uses inverse weighting based on an upper bound on occupancy, a quantity describing visitation during interaction. These two components address uncertainty about transitions and the challenge of estimating losses from the feedback that is actually available.

The authors prove a high-probability regret bound of order L times the number of states times the square root of the number of actions times the number of episodes, suppressing logarithmic factors. They identify this as the first square-root-in-episodes guarantee for this setting. Its order matches the cited full-information result, despite the more restricted feedback available here.
icml-2020-learning-adversarial-markov-de.tldr: An efficient algorithm achieves high-probability square-root regret for adversarial episodic decision processes with unknown transitions and bandit feedback.

paragraphs: High-level planning requires a useful abstraction of the detailed environment in which an agent acts. If that abstraction must be learned separately for every task, transferring to a new problem can require substantial additional experience. This paper proposes learning a portable representation that describes a collection of continuous, low-level environments.

The representation is learned in an agent-specific, egocentric space that does not depend on the particular task. It includes a symbolic vocabulary and operators expressed using that vocabulary. For each new task, the agent learns how to instantiate those operators with problem-specific information, separating reusable planning concepts from their particular application.

The authors show that the abstract representations are provably sufficient for planning when grounded with the required problem-specific information. They also demonstrate transfer in two domains, reporting fewer samples needed to learn a representation for a new task. The guarantee therefore concerns grounded representations; portability does not eliminate the task-specific learning needed to connect the shared vocabulary and operators to a particular problem.
icml-2020-learning-portable-representati.tldr: Reusable symbolic representations reduce new-task learning needs and are sufficient for planning when grounded with problem-specific information.

paragraphs: Molecule generation for drug discovery often requires satisfying several chemical-property constraints at once. As more constraints are added, sampling compounds in their intersection becomes increasingly difficult. This paper approaches that challenge by building around interpretable molecular substructures associated with the individual properties of interest.

The authors call these substructures molecular rationales. They identify them within molecules as pieces likely to account for a desired property, then train graph generative models to expand them into complete molecules. The final generator combines multiple rationale completions through a mixture model and fine-tunes that mixture to preserve the target properties.

This design gives property-related substructures an explicit role in generation, rather than leaving the entire multi-property problem to an undifferentiated molecular representation. Evaluations on several drug-design tasks show significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy, diversity, and novelty of generated compounds. The rationales are described as likely contributors to properties, so their interpretability should not be read as proof that each substructure causally guarantees its associated property.
icml-2020-multi-objective-molecule-gener.tldr: The model expands property-associated molecular substructures into compounds, improving multi-objective generation in accuracy, diversity, and novelty.

paragraphs: Estimating a discrete distribution means learning how probability is spread across distinct possible outcomes. In many applications, observations arrive in batches rather than as one undifferentiated dataset. The paper considers the difficult case where some batches may be unreliable, faulty, or deliberately adversarial, so the estimator must tolerate corrupted groups of observations.

Earlier estimators for this setting required exponential running time. In some regimes, they also needed more batches than were optimal. These are separate obstacles: an estimator can demand too much computation even when enough data are available, or require too much data even if its calculation could otherwise be performed.

The authors provide the first polynomial-time estimator for this setting that is optimal in the number of batches and achieves essentially the best possible estimation accuracy. The result addresses computational cost, batch requirements, and accuracy together. Its relevance extends to the batched-data settings named in the abstract, including sensor networks, collaborative filtering, natural language processing, and federated learning, where unreliable data sources can complicate distribution estimation.
icml-2020-optimal-robust-learning-of-dis.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial-time estimator for corrupted batches that uses an optimal number of batches and achieves essentially optimal accuracy.

paragraphs: A model’s evaluation metric may be difficult to optimize directly, especially when its mathematical formula is unavailable. This paper tackles that problem by expressing the metric as a monotonic function of a small collection of easier-to-optimize surrogate quantities. Those surrogates provide a manageable space in which to guide training.

The method formulates optimization over a relaxed surrogate space, estimates local gradients of the desired metric, and performs inexact convex projections. The authors analyze two ways to estimate the gradients: finite differences and local linear interpolation. Both use local information about how the metric changes rather than requiring its full mathematical expression.

The convergence analysis assumes smoothness with respect to the surrogates, so the guarantee depends on structure in the relationship between those quantities and the metric. Experiments on classification and ranking show performance comparable to methods given the metric’s formula, with notable value when the formula is unknown. The contribution is an adaptive route from accessible surrogate objectives to a harder or opaque evaluation target.
icml-2020-optimizing-black-box-metrics-w.tldr: The method optimizes difficult or unknown metrics through a small surrogate space, with convergence under stated smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Scalable Gaussian-process methods make regression feasible on large datasets, but their uncertainty estimates can be too small. The paper identifies a particular problem: predictive variance can be dominated by observation noise, leaving too little contribution from uncertainty about the function itself. That weakens the input-dependent uncertainty modeling that makes Gaussian processes appealing.

The authors propose two methods to address this. The first applies variational inference to the Fully Independent Training Conditional approximation, or FITC. The second directly targets the posterior predictive distribution instead of constructing a posterior approximation first. Both are intended to improve predictive uncertainty while retaining scalability.

An extensive empirical comparison with alternative scalable Gaussian-process regressors finds better-calibrated uncertainty and higher predictive log likelihoods. The reported likelihood gains are often as large as half a nat per data point. These findings concern the quality of the predictive distribution, including how uncertainty is assigned, rather than merely whether its central prediction is close to the observed value.
icml-2020-parametric-gaussian-process-re.tldr: Two scalable Gaussian-process regression methods improve uncertainty calibration and predictive likelihood in extensive empirical comparisons.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates learning about an environment from choosing what to achieve in it. During exploration, the agent collects trajectories without a predetermined reward function. Afterwards, it uses that experience to compute policies for supplied rewards. This is useful when many objectives matter or another agent later specifies the desired behavior.

The algorithm finds exploratory policies that collectively visit each significant state with probability proportional to the greatest visitation probability achievable by any policy. This organizes exploration around which states can meaningfully be reached. The subsequent planning step can use a black-box approximate planner, including value iteration or natural policy gradient.

The authors guarantee epsilon-suboptimal policies for arbitrarily many reward functions after an exploration budget scaling as S squared times A times a polynomial in H, divided by epsilon squared, up to logarithmic factors. Here S counts states, A actions, and H the horizon. A nearly matching lower bound establishes near-optimality in this setting, although the stated upper and lower bounds do not specify identical horizon dependence.
icml-2020-reward-free-exploration-for-re.tldr: Reward-free exploration gathers reusable experience for many later reward functions with a provably near-optimal exploration budget.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines examples with labels and examples without them. FlowGMM approaches this through a generative model built from a normalizing flow: an invertible neural transformation that connects data to a latent distribution while keeping likelihood exactly computable. The latent distribution is a Gaussian mixture, giving the model a structured space in which to represent data.

The approach trains end to end and treats labeled and unlabeled observations within one likelihood-based framework. Its appeal is the combination of a relatively simple construction, interpretable latent structure, and applicability beyond images. Exact likelihood supplies a common modeling basis for the two kinds of training data.

The authors report promising results on AG-News and Yahoo Answers text, tabular datasets, and semi-supervised image classification. They also show that the model can uncover interpretable structure, produce real-time feature visualizations without additional optimization, and yield well-calibrated predictive distributions. These findings present FlowGMM as a broadly applicable semi-supervised approach, with demonstrated interpretability and uncertainty-related capabilities alongside classification results.
icml-2020-semi-supervised-learning-with-.tldr: FlowGMM combines normalizing flows with a latent Gaussian mixture to learn jointly from labeled and unlabeled data across several data types.

paragraphs: Source separation tries to recover the components that were combined into an observed mixture. For richly structured signals, separated outputs can still contain visible artifacts. This paper uses deep generative models to describe plausible individual sources, bringing their ability to represent realistic data into a Bayesian separation procedure.

The generative models serve as priors over the mixture’s components. Given a mixture, the method samples from the posterior distribution of possible sources using noise-annealed Langevin dynamics. This separates the task of building a good generative model from the task of recovering sources, allowing advances in generative modeling to be used directly as priors.

The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on MNIST digit separation. For richer image data, the authors introduce evaluation methodology and provide quantitative evaluation and qualitative discussion on CIFAR-10, along with qualitative results on LSUN. The evidence therefore has different forms across datasets: the abstract’s explicit state-of-the-art claim concerns MNIST, while the richer datasets support a broader examination of separation quality.
icml-2020-source-separation-with-deep-ge.tldr: The method separates mixtures by using deep generative priors and posterior sampling, achieving state-of-the-art MNIST separation results.

paragraphs: As GAN-generated images become more realistic, the artifacts that help detectors recognize them become less obvious. A detector may also struggle to transfer what it learned about one kind of generated image to another. T-GD addresses this transfer problem through a teacher-and-student framework designed to improve detection while preserving earlier knowledge.

The teacher first learns from a source dataset and provides the starting point for learning on a target dataset. Student training introduces noise by mixing source and target data, while constraining changes in the weights to retain that starting point. Teacher and student then iteratively teach and evaluate one another within a self-training process.

The authors report strong performance on the source data while overcoming catastrophic forgetting, together with effective detection of state-of-the-art GAN images using a small amount of data and no metadata. The method’s distinguishing focus is transferring detection knowledge. Its training design connects adaptation to new generated images with preservation of the detector’s ability on the source dataset.
icml-2020-t-gd-transferable-gan-generate.tldr: T-GD uses teacher-student self-training to transfer GAN-image detection to new data while preserving performance on the source dataset.

paragraphs: A generative model must represent not only typical observations but also the tails of a distribution, where extreme values occur. This paper studies how triangular transformations in normalizing flows change tail behavior. It connects the slope needed in the transformation to density quantile functions of the source and target distributions.

The authors show that a Lipschitz-continuous transport map preserves similar tail properties to those of its source distribution. This creates a tradeoff: achieving the desired target tails depends on both the source distribution and the transformation’s expressiveness. They illustrate that Real-NVP, MAF, and Glow, as implemented in the examined setting, cannot capture distributions with non-Gaussian tails.

To address this, the paper proposes tail-adaptive flows that learn the source distribution alongside the triangular map. The starting distribution can therefore adjust its tail behavior instead of leaving all adaptation to the transformation. Synthetic and real-world experiments complement the theory. The architectural limitation is stated for the implementations examined, rather than for every possible modification of those flow families.
icml-2020-tails-of-lipschitz-triangular-.tldr: The paper characterizes tail restrictions in Lipschitz flows and proposes learning the source distribution to better capture target tails.
